---
title: "spellcheck.yml"
---

Spellcheck an R package's prose with the
[{spelling}](https://docs.ropensci.org/spelling/) package.
The package's own `inst/WORDLIST` is the accepted vocabulary, so a repo
migrating from a bespoke `check-spelling.yaml` keeps its wordlist unchanged --
that file is {spelling}'s own format.

## What it reads

`spell_check_package()` decides the population, and it is narrower than "the
repo's prose" in one direction and wider in another.
Read off `spell_check_package()`'s source at {spelling} 2.3.2 and confirmed
against a fixture (2026-08-21):

- `DESCRIPTION`'s `Title` and `Description` fields, and no other field.
- Every `man/*.Rd` help page.
- Vignette sources under `vignettes/`, matched as `.md`/`.Rmd`/`.qmd`, plus
  `.Rnw`/`.Snw`. These are parsed as text, never rendered, which is why
  `install-quarto` defaults to `'false'` even for a `.qmd` vignette.
- Root-level Markdown whose name matches `readme`, `news`, `changes`, or
  `index`, case-insensitively. So a package's own `README.md` and `NEWS.md`
  **are** checked.

Everything else is out of reach: a Quarto site's other pages, `CONTRIBUTING.md`,
code comments, YAML, and any repository that is not an R package at all.
[gha#557](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/issues/557) tracks covering those
with a separate tool.

The package's own name and its authors' names are added to the accepted
vocabulary automatically, so neither needs a `WORDLIST` entry.

Add a newly-accepted word with `spelling::update_wordlist()` in the package,
and commit the result.

## Inputs

| Input                | Type   | Default       | Description                                                          |
| -------------------- | ------ | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `path`               | string | `'.'`         | Path to the package root, relative to the repository.                |
| `exclude`            | string | `''`          | Comma-separated files or folders to skip. Accepts globs.             |
| `additional-options` | string | `'--vanilla'` | Options passed to `Rscript`. Pass `''` to let R read its profiles.   |
| `install-quarto`     | string | `'false'`     | Whether dependency setup installs Quarto.                            |
| `runs-on`            | string | `ubuntu-latest` | Runner label for the job.                                          |

## Permissions

Only `contents: read` (the default), so no `permissions:` block is needed.

## Example

```yaml
name: Spellcheck
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:
jobs:
  spellcheck:
    uses: Morrison-Lab/gha/.github/workflows/spellcheck.yml@v2
    # with:
    #   path: '.'
    #   exclude: 'vignettes/*.Rmd'
    #   additional-options: ''
    #   install-quarto: 'auto'
```

See the [`examples/`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/tree/main/examples)
directory for the full caller stub (`spellcheck.yml`).

## Why it sets up R instead of running in a container

The bespoke workflows this replaces run inside a `rocker` image.
This one calls
[`r-lib/actions/setup-r`](https://github.com/r-lib/actions/tree/v2/setup-r),
matching every other R capability here, so a consumer already paying for
`setup-r` in its other jobs reuses that toolchain cache.

It also installs {spelling} through
[`setup-r-dependencies`](https://github.com/r-lib/actions/tree/v2/setup-r-dependencies)
rather than leaving it to the upstream action's own `install.packages()` call.
That call sets `repos` to `cloud.r-project.org`, which serves source packages
for Linux, so it would compile {spelling} and its {hunspell} C++ dependency on
every run.
Going through `setup-r-dependencies` takes the public RSPM binaries instead and
caches them, and the upstream install then finds the package present.

Only {spelling} is installed, not the consumer package's own dependencies:
`spell_check_package()` reads a package's files without loading it, so
resolving its dependency tree would be pure cost.
For the same reason `install-quarto` defaults to `'false'` -- {spelling} reads
vignette *sources* and never renders them.

## Three upstream behaviours worth knowing

This capability wraps
[`insightsengineering/r-spellcheck-action`](https://github.com/insightsengineering/r-spellcheck-action),
which carries three quirks a caller can be bitten by.
All were confirmed by reading and running its `action.yaml` and `spellcheck.R`
at `v3.0.3` (2026-08-21), not inferred from its documentation.

**A lone glob in `exclude` used to exclude only its first match -- this
capability works around that.**
Upstream interpolates `exclude` unquoted into a `bash` `run:` body, so the
shell pathname-expands it into separate arguments before R sees it, and
`spellcheck.R` reads only the first.
Measured over three vignettes: `vignettes/*.Rmd` excluded
`vignettes/a.Rmd` and left the other two checked, silently.
The composite therefore normalizes the value first -- entries trimmed,
rejoined with commas, and given a trailing comma -- which the shell cannot
expand, since no path ends in a comma.
R's own `Sys.glob()` then does the matching, so a glob excludes every file it
matches, as the input has always claimed.
The one shape that cannot be supported is an entry containing whitespace: the
shell splits on it whatever we do, so such an entry is rejected with an error
naming it.

**`exclude` deletes the files it matches.**
The script calls `file.remove()` on each glob match, and the branch meant to
restore them afterwards tests `isTRUE()` against the *list* `lapply()` returned,
which is never true.
So excluded files stay deleted from the runner's checkout for the rest of the
job.
That is harmless in a job that only spellchecks, which is why the caller stub
does nothing else -- but do not add steps after it that read or publish the
working tree.

**A count of exactly 256 misspelled words reports success.**
The script exits with the misspelling count as its status, and a process exit
status is taken modulo 256, so 256 words becomes `0`.
Measured on R 4.6.1: `quit(status = 256)` is observed by the shell as `0`.
Any count from 1 to 255 fails correctly, so this only reaches a package
adopting the check with a very large wordlist gap.
[gha#556](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/gha/issues/556) tracks reporting it
upstream and deciding whether to guard it here.
